title: Node, npm and Express
blurb: The runtime, the module system, middleware, streams and the npm ecosystem — what a fullstack interview expects you to know about the server side of JavaScript.

questions.q: What does Node give your code that a browser tab does not?
choices: An event loop, so async callbacks can run without blocking the thread
Filesystem, process and raw socket APIs such as fs, child_process and net
Native promises and async/await, which older browsers only get via polyfills
A built-in JSON parser and fetch(), which browsers leave to libraries
questions.why: Both run a JavaScript engine with an event loop, promises, JSON and (since Node 18) fetch. Node adds the OS-facing APIs and drops the DOM, window and localStorage, which is why "window is not defined" shows up during server-side rendering.
questions.asked: A warm-up that checks you know the event loop is shared and the difference is the host APIs.

questions.q: What is the difference between `dependencies` and `devDependencies`?
choices: devDependencies are installed globally; dependencies go in the local node_modules
dependencies are pinned by the lockfile; devDependencies float within their range
dependencies are needed at runtime; devDependencies only to build, lint and test
devDependencies are bundled into the build output; dependencies load at runtime
questions.why: `npm ci --omit=dev` in a production image skips devDependencies, giving a smaller, less exposed container. Both kinds are local and both are locked by package-lock.json. Putting TypeScript or a test runner in dependencies is a common slip.
questions.asked: Checks you have built a production image rather than only run `npm install` on a laptop.

questions.q: What does a committed `package-lock.json` guarantee?
choices: That every package in the tree has passed npm's malware and audit checks
That npm install always fetches the newest version each range allows
Only faster installs, because npm can skip downloading the tarballs
The exact resolved version and integrity hash of every package in the tree
questions.why: Without a lockfile, `^1.2.0` can resolve to a different 1.x on the CI machine than on yours. The lockfile says nothing about safety: a locked version can still be malicious. Use `npm ci` in CI; it installs strictly from the lockfile and fails if package.json disagrees.
questions.asked: Follow-up: "what is the difference between npm install and npm ci?"

questions.q: Which versions does the range `^1.2.3` allow?
choices: Only patch releases of 1.2, from 1.2.3 up to but excluding 1.3.0
Any release at or above 1.2.3, including 2.x and later majors
Any 1.x.y at or above 1.2.3: new minors and patches, never 2.0.0
Exactly 1.2.3, unless npm update is run with the --latest flag
questions.why: The caret allows anything that does not change the leftmost non-zero part; `~1.2.3` is the patch-only range. Semver's promise that minors are compatible holds often enough to be useful and not always enough to skip the lockfile. Note `^0.2.3` allows only 0.2.x.
questions.asked: Leads to "so why did a minor update break production?" and the lockfile.

questions.q: What is Express middleware?
choices: A plugin registered once at startup that Express calls for each route file
A wrapper Express puts around database calls to manage their connections
A hook that runs after the response is sent, for logging and cleanup
A (req, res, next) function in an ordered chain that handles or passes on
questions.why: Order is everything: a body parser registered after a route means `req.body` is undefined there, and an auth middleware registered after a route does not protect it. Middleware can run code after the response too, but that is one use, not the definition.
questions.asked: The follow-up is always "what happens if you register it after the routes?"

questions.q: Why does this error handler never run?
choices: Error handlers take three parameters, so the extra err makes Express skip it
It must call next(err) itself, or Express treats the error as unhandled
It is registered before the route, so errors thrown there never reach it
res.status() is not available inside error handlers, so the call throws
questions.why: Express walks the stack in registration order, and an error only travels forward to error handlers registered after the point where it happened. Error handlers are recognised by having four parameters; dropping `next` turns one into ordinary middleware.
questions.asked: A code-review classic; the four-parameter rule is the follow-up.

questions.q: In Express 4, why does a rejected promise in an async route handler not reach the error handler?
choices: Express 4 ignores the returned promise, so you must catch and call next(err)
The error handler must itself be declared async to receive rejected promises
Express 4 forwards rejections only when the value is an instance of Error
Express 4 rejects async functions as route handlers when routes are registered
questions.why: Express 4 calls the handler and discards what it returns, so the rejection is unhandled: since Node 15 that crashes the process by default (`--unhandled-rejections=throw`), and if an `unhandledRejection` handler is registered the request hangs until the client times out instead. Wrap handlers in a helper that attaches `.catch(next)`, or move to Express 5, which forwards rejected promises to the error handler.
questions.asked: A very practical Express question: this bug produces either a crashed process or mysterious hanging requests, depending on how unhandled rejections are configured.

questions.q: In Node 24, how do CommonJS and ES modules differ?
choices: require loads synchronously at run time; import is statically analysed and hoisted
ESM is browser-only syntax, so Node rewrites every import into a require call
CommonJS was removed in Node 22, so require only works behind a runtime flag
Nothing that matters: each loads the other freely, with no caveats whatsoever
questions.why: Static imports enable tree shaking and top-level await. Node picks the loader by extension, the package "type" field, or (since 22.7) syntax detection. `require()` of an ES module works unflagged since 22.12, but not for a graph with top-level await, so interop still has a caveat. In ESM, `__dirname` is `import.meta.dirname`.
questions.asked: Checks your module knowledge is current: older answers say ESM needs "type": "module" and require(esm) is impossible.

questions.q: Why stream a large file to the client rather than read it into memory first?
choices: Streams are always faster, because they bypass the kernel's page cache
fs.readFile refuses any file over 100 MB, so a stream is the only option
A stream moves the file in chunks, so memory stays flat per request
Streams gzip the data on the fly, so less of it crosses the network
questions.why: Ten concurrent requests each buffering a 500 MB file is 5 GB of RAM and an OOM kill. Streams also start sending immediately, so time to first byte improves. They are not inherently faster in throughput, and `readFile` only fails near 2 GiB.
questions.asked: Checks you think about memory per request, not per process, once concurrency is involved.

questions.q: What is backpressure in a Node stream?
choices: The consumer signalling it is full, so the producer pauses until it drains
An error in the destination travelling back upstream to close the source
The internal buffer spilling over to disk once it grows past highWaterMark
The retry a writable stream performs when a write to the socket fails
questions.why: When `write()` returns false the producer should wait for `drain`. Ignore it and you buffer a fast source in memory while a slow destination crawls. `pipeline()` handles backpressure and error propagation for you; hand-rolled `on('data')` loops usually do not.
questions.asked: Separates people who have piped a real upload or export from people who have read about streams.

questions.q: How should configuration reach a Node service in production?
choices: A config.json per environment, committed and selected by NODE_ENV
Constants per environment, compiled into the build by the bundler
Command-line flags only, so the running config is visible in ps
Environment variables validated at startup, secrets from a store
questions.why: Environment config is the twelve-factor default and what containers and CI expect. Validate at boot and crash loudly: discovering a missing DATABASE_URL on the first request at 3am is much worse than at deploy. Flags in `ps` leak secrets to anyone on the host.
questions.asked: Tests whether one build artefact can move unchanged through every environment.

questions.q: What happens by default when an exception is never caught in Node?
choices: Node logs the stack trace and carries on with the next queued event
The process exits with an error, and a supervisor should restart it
Express's error middleware catches it and returns a 500 to the client
The event loop restarts, dropping pending callbacks but keeping state
questions.why: After an uncaught exception the application state is unknown, so log, flush and exit, and let the orchestrator start a clean process. Express only catches what is thrown synchronously in its handlers (and, in Express 5, rejected promises); a throw inside a timer or event callback escapes it.
questions.asked: The follow-up is whether keeping the process alive with an uncaughtException handler is a good idea (it is not).

questions.q: How do you use more than one CPU core with a Node web service?
choices: Nothing to do: libuv spreads your JavaScript across every core itself
Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE so more of your JavaScript runs in parallel
Run several processes (cluster or containers); worker_threads for CPU work
Convert handlers to async/await so each request gets its own OS thread
questions.why: JavaScript executes on one thread per process. The libuv pool runs some native I/O and crypto work, not your code, so resizing it does not parallelise handlers. Most services scale by running N containers behind a load balancer, which also gives restarts and rolling deploys.
questions.asked: Checks you know the single-threaded model and how production actually scales it.

questions.q: What blocks the Node event loop?
choices: Synchronous CPU work or sync I/O such as fs.readFileSync in a handler
Every await, because the whole process pauses until the promise settles
Database queries, because the driver waits for the network reply
Large responses, because res.send waits for the client to download
questions.why: Async I/O is handed to the OS or the libuv pool, and the loop serves other requests meanwhile; `await` suspends only the current function. A single two-second JSON.parse of a huge payload stalls every concurrent request on that process.
questions.asked: Then: "so how would you handle a CPU-heavy endpoint?" A worker thread, a queue, or a different runtime.

questions.q: What is the difference between a liveness check and a readiness check?
choices: Liveness checks the database is reachable; readiness checks the port is open
Liveness runs once at startup; readiness runs again on every incoming request
They are the same probe, except readiness also reports the deployed version
Liveness asks whether to restart the process; readiness whether to send it traffic
questions.why: A failed liveness check means "this process is wedged, restart it"; a failed readiness check means "do not route to me right now" (warming up, dependency down). Putting a database check in liveness means a brief database blip restarts every instance at once.
questions.asked: Checks you have seen a restart storm, or can reason about one.

questions.q: Where should request validation happen in an Express API?
choices: In database constraints only, since they are the final authority
In the frontend form, since that is where users enter the data
At the boundary, before the handler's logic or any database call
Wherever each value is first used, deep in the service layer
questions.why: Validate once at the boundary and the rest of the code can trust its inputs. Constraints are a last line of defence with poor error messages, and client-side validation is a UX feature: anyone can post directly to your API.
questions.asked: Checks you treat the client as untrusted and know where the trust boundary is.

questions.q: What is the risk of a transitive dependency you never chose?
choices: None, provided the direct dependency comes from a trusted publisher
It only lengthens install time, since unused code is never loaded
A compromised deep package runs with your process's full privileges
npm refuses packages not listed directly in your package.json
questions.why: Install scripts and runtime code both execute as your process, with its network, filesystem and secrets. Mitigations: pin with a lockfile, audit in CI, prefer fewer well-maintained dependencies, and consider `--ignore-scripts`.
questions.asked: Supply-chain incidents are now a routine interview topic; the lockfile and install scripts are the follow-ups.

questions.q: In Express, what does `res.json(data)` do that `res.send(JSON.stringify(data))` does not?
choices: It streams the body in chunks instead of buffering the whole string
It skips building the string first, so it serialises noticeably faster
Nothing: both send the same bytes with the same response headers
It sets Content-Type to application/json and applies the app's JSON settings
questions.why: `res.send` with a string sets `Content-Type: text/html`, so clients that branch on the header treat the body as text. `res.json` sets the JSON type and honours the `json replacer` and `json spaces` settings. It still builds the whole string in memory.
questions.asked: Small, but it is the cause of "the response is a string" bugs on the client.

questions.q: What does graceful shutdown mean for a Node web service?
choices: Restarting the process automatically whenever it exits with an error
Flushing buffered logs in an uncaughtException handler just before exiting
Closing the database pool first, so that no new queries can start
On SIGTERM: stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close pools, exit
questions.why: During a rolling deploy the orchestrator sends SIGTERM and waits. Exiting immediately drops requests mid-flight; closing the pool first makes the in-flight requests fail instead. `server.close()` stops new connections and calls back when the existing ones finish.
questions.asked: A strong signal for anyone claiming deployment experience.

questions.q: How should a production Node service write its logs?
choices: console.log lines to a file that the app itself rotates each day
Errors only, because info-level logs cost too much to ship and store
Full request and response bodies, so that any bug can be replayed
Structured JSON to stdout, with levels and a request correlation id
questions.why: Containers collect stdout, so the app should not manage files, and structured logs are queryable. Info logs are what reconstruct a request; bodies leak passwords, tokens and card numbers.
questions.asked: Leads to what you must never log, and how you find one request across services.

questions.q: In Express 5, what does `app.use(express.json())` do with an incoming request?
choices: Parses every request body as JSON, whatever its Content-Type header says
Parses bodies with a JSON Content-Type into req.body, up to 100kb by default
Validates JSON bodies against the route's schema and rejects bad ones with 400
Parses JSON bodies of any size, and serialises every res.send() as JSON too
questions.why: It only acts when the Content-Type matches application/json; otherwise `req.body` stays undefined in Express 5 (Express 4 set it to `{}`). Bodies over the 100kb default are rejected with 413 and malformed JSON with 400. Raise the limit on the routes that need it rather than globally.
questions.asked: Checks you know the parser is conditional and bounded, which explains both "req.body is undefined" and "413" tickets.

questions.q: Why is `path.join(baseDir, req.query.file)` dangerous in a download route?
choices: path.join is synchronous, so it blocks the event loop on each request
Input such as ../../etc/passwd resolves outside the intended folder
path.join follows symlinks, so it can reach any file on the disk
path.join does not normalise separators, so Windows paths break
questions.why: `path.join` resolves `..` segments, so it happily walks out of `baseDir`. Resolve the path, then check it still starts with the base directory, or map input to an allowlist of names. It is a pure string operation: fast, and it never touches the filesystem.
questions.asked: Path traversal is the Node-specific injection interviewers expect you to spot in review.

questions.q: What does `express.Router()` give you in a growing Express app?
choices: A separate HTTP server per feature, each listening on its own port
Routes generated automatically from the files in a routes/ folder
A mini-app with its own routes and middleware, mounted at a path prefix
A registry that loads each route file lazily on its first request
questions.why: `app.use('/orders', ordersRouter)` mounts a router so its paths are relative to the prefix, and middleware added to that router (auth, validation) applies only to its routes. Express has no file-based routing; that is a feature of other frameworks.
questions.asked: Checks you can structure a codebase past one index.js.

questions.q: A client requests `GET /users/42?tab=orders`. What does this handler see?
choices: req.params.id is '42' and req.query.tab is 'orders'
req.params.id is 42 and req.query.tab is 'orders'
req.query.id is '42' and req.params.tab is 'orders'
req.body.id is '42' and req.query.tab is 'orders'
questions.why: Path segments named in the route land in `req.params`, the query string in `req.query`, and `req.body` is only filled by a body parser. Everything from the URL is a string, so `42` must be parsed and validated before it is used as a number.
questions.asked: A junior screen favourite; the string-not-number detail is what the interviewer is listening for.

questions.q: Your build emits hashed filenames such as `app.3f9a.js`. How should `express.static` cache them?
choices: With no-store, so users can never run an outdated JavaScript bundle
With a long max-age and immutable, since a changed file gets a new name
With no Cache-Control header at all, so each browser picks a sensible default
With max-age=0 on the assets and a long max-age on index.html itself
questions.why: A content hash means the URL changes whenever the bytes do, so a year-long `max-age` with `immutable` is safe. `express.static` defaults to `max-age=0` with an ETag, so every load revalidates. Keep index.html revalidated (the reverse of the last option), or users never see the new hashes.
questions.asked: Checks you connect bundler output to HTTP caching, which is where "users see the old version" tickets come from.

questions.q: What does adding the `helmet` middleware to an Express app do?
choices: Validates and sanitises request bodies against injection attacks
Rate-limits each client IP to stop brute force and denial of service
Encrypts cookies and session data with a key from the environment
Sets security response headers such as CSP, HSTS and nosniff
questions.why: Helmet sets headers like Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security and X-Content-Type-Options, and removes X-Powered-By. It does nothing to requests: validation, rate limiting and cookie signing are separate middleware.
questions.asked: Checks you know what a common dependency actually does rather than treating it as "security, done".

questions.q: Why does `express-session` with its default store break once you run three instances behind a load balancer?
choices: The default MemoryStore lives in one process, so the others lack the session
The cookie is signed per instance, so the other two reject its signature
Each session holds a row lock in the database, so the instances deadlock
Sessions are tied to one TCP connection, which the balancer does not reuse
questions.why: Each process has its own MemoryStore, so a request that lands on another instance looks logged out. The docs also warn MemoryStore leaks and is not for production. Use a shared store such as Redis or the database; sticky sessions only hide the problem until an instance restarts.
questions.asked: A direct test of whether you have scaled a stateful Express app past one instance.

questions.q: Requests for a missing order log 'Cannot set headers after they are sent'. Why?
choices: db.find resolved after Express had already sent a default response
res.status() sends the headers at once, before json() can add its own
The 404 branch has no return, so res.json(order) also runs after it
Async handlers must call next() after responding, or Express resends
questions.why: The 404 is sent, execution falls through, and the second `res.json` tries to set headers on a finished response. Write `return res.status(404).json(...)`. `res.status()` only sets the code; nothing is sent until `json()` or `send()`.
questions.asked: One of the most common Express errors in real logs; spotting the missing return in review is the skill.

questions.q: Behind a load balancer, `req.ip` is always the balancer's address and `req.secure` is false. What is the Express fix?
choices: Read `req.headers['x-forwarded-for']` in each handler yourself and take its first entry as the client
Set `app.set('trust proxy', 1)`, so Express reads X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto
Enable `app.enable('https')` so Express knows the client connection was TLS-terminated upstream
Mount the app on `https.createServer` with the balancer's certificate, so req.secure becomes true
questions.why: Express only honours the X-Forwarded-* headers when `trust proxy` says which hops to believe; `1` trusts the nearest proxy, after which `req.ip`, `req.ips`, `req.protocol` and `req.secure` describe the original client. Reading the header yourself lets any client forge its IP, which breaks rate limiting and audit logs; trusting every hop (`true`) has the same flaw if the app is reachable directly. There is no `https` setting, and the app's own TLS is irrelevant because the balancer terminated it.
questions.asked: The Express version of the forwarded-headers question; wrong values break secure cookies, redirects and per-IP rate limits.

questions.q: In Express 5, what happens when this route is registered?
questions.code: app.get('*', (req, res) => res.sendFile(indexHtml));
choices: It matches every GET path, exactly as it did in Express 4
It throws at startup: a wildcard needs a name, such as /*splat
It only matches the literal path /*, since * is no longer special
It matches a single segment, so /a/b falls through to a 404
questions.why: Express 5 uses path-to-regexp v8, where a bare `*` is a syntax error ("Missing parameter name"). Write `/*splat` (one or more segments) or `/{*splat}` to also match the root. The "matches the literal path" idea is wrong because the parser rejects it before any request arrives.
questions.asked: The most common breakage when upgrading an SPA fallback route from Express 4 to 5.

questions.q: In Express 5, how do you declare one route that matches both `/users` and `/users/42`?
choices: app.get('/users/:id?', handler)
app.get('/users/(:id)', handler)
app.get('/users{/:id}', handler)
app.get('/users/:id*', handler)
questions.why: Express 5 marks optional parts with braces, so `{/:id}` makes the slash and parameter optional together. The Express 4 form `:id?` now throws "Unexpected ?" when the route is registered, and parentheses and `*` modifiers are no longer valid in path strings.
questions.asked: Tells the interviewer whether your Express knowledge is from before or after the v5 path syntax change.

questions.q: What does `GET /users/me` return?
questions.code:
app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => res.send(`id=${req.params.id}`));
app.get('/users/me', (req, res) => res.send('me'));
choices: me, because a literal segment always outranks a parameter
A 404, because the two routes conflict and both are skipped
id=me, because the first matching route in order wins
An error at startup, because the two paths overlap
questions.why: Express has no specificity ranking: it walks routes in registration order and the first match handles the request, so `:id` captures "me". Register `/users/me` first. Frameworks such as Fastify do rank static segments above parameters, which is where the "literal wins" belief comes from.
questions.asked: A classic "why is my /me endpoint hitting the wrong handler" bug that shows you know routing is ordered.

questions.q: What does `GET /a?skip=1` return?
choices: first
second
third
questions.why: `next('route')` skips the remaining callbacks of the current route and moves to the next matching route, so 'second' is bypassed and the second `app.get('/a')` answers. Plain `next()` would have run 'second'.
questions.asked: Checks you know the difference between next(), next(err) and next("route").

questions.q: In Express 5 with default settings, what is `req.query` for `GET /q?user[name]=x&tag=a&tag=b`?
choices: { user: { name: 'x' }, tag: ['a', 'b'] }
{ 'user[name]': 'x', tag: 'b' }
{ user: { name: 'x' }, tag: 'a,b' }
{ 'user[name]': 'x', tag: ['a', 'b'] }
questions.why: Express 5 switched the default query parser from `qs` ("extended") to Node's `querystring` ("simple"): brackets are not expanded into nested objects, but repeated keys still become an array. Nested parsing needs `app.set('query parser', 'extended')`, the Express 4 default.
questions.asked: Shows you know a silent default changed in v5 and that query values can be arrays, not just strings.

questions.q: A search route does `req.query.tag.toLowerCase()`. It works in testing, then throws `TypeError: toLowerCase is not a function` in production. What request caused it?
choices: One with ?tag= and an empty value, which Express parses to null
One with ?tag=a&tag=b, which Express parses to an array
One with ?tag=123, which Express parses to a number
One with ?TAG=a, which leaves req.query.tag undefined
questions.why: Query values are strings, arrays of strings (for repeated keys) or undefined; Express never converts to numbers or null. An array has no `toLowerCase`. Validate the query with a schema instead of trusting its shape; a missing key would throw "Cannot read properties of undefined" instead.
questions.asked: Checks you treat the query string as untrusted input with a shape the client controls.

questions.q: In an Express 5 ES module, a validation middleware does `req.query = schema.parse(req.query)`. What happens?
choices: It works: later handlers see the parsed, typed values
It is ignored in dev mode but applied when NODE_ENV=production
It throws a TypeError, because req.query is a getter with no setter
It works, but Express re-parses the URL on the next read
questions.why: In Express 5 `req.query` is a getter, so assigning to it throws in strict-mode code (every ES module) and is silently ignored in sloppy CommonJS. Store the parsed result elsewhere, for example `res.locals.query` or a typed `req.validated`. `req.body` is still a plain writable property.
questions.asked: A real upgrade bug in validation middleware; knowing it shows you have written one against v5.

questions.q: In Express 5, what is `req.body` in this handler for a JSON POST?
questions.code:
app.post('/orders', (req, res) => res.json({ body: req.body }));
app.use(express.json());
choices: The parsed JSON object, since middleware order does not matter
An empty object {}, because nothing has parsed the body yet
The raw JSON string, since express.json has not run yet
undefined, because the parser is registered after the route
questions.why: Middleware runs in registration order, so the route handles the request before `express.json()` ever sees it. Express 5 leaves `req.body` undefined when no parser has run; Express 4 defaulted it to `{}`, which is where the empty-object answer comes from.
questions.asked: The most common "req.body is undefined" cause, and a quick test of whether you know order is behaviour.

questions.q: With `app.use(express.json())`, a client POSTs a valid JSON string but sends `Content-Type: text/plain`. What is `req.body`?
choices: The parsed object, because the parser sniffs the content
undefined, because the parser only handles JSON types
The raw string, because text bodies pass through as-is
A 415 error is sent before the route handler runs
questions.why: `express.json()` checks the Content-Type against its `type` option (default `application/json`) and calls `next()` untouched when it does not match, so in Express 5 `req.body` stays undefined. It does not sniff, does not produce a string (that is `express.text()`), and does not reject with 415.
questions.asked: Debugging a client that forgot the header is a routine support task for API developers.

questions.q: A client sends 2 MB of JSON to an app using `express.json()` with default options. What happens?
choices: The body is parsed in full, since the limit only applies to uploads
The first 100kb is parsed and the remainder is silently discarded
The request hangs until the client gives up and closes the socket
next() receives an error with status 413 and type entity.too.large
questions.why: The default `limit` is 100kb; bigger bodies become an error with `status: 413` and `type: 'entity.too.large'` that flows to your error handler. The parser never truncates, because half a JSON document is not valid JSON. Raise the limit per route rather than globally.
questions.asked: Checks you know body limits exist and how the error reaches your handler.

questions.q: A client sends `{bad json` with `Content-Type: application/json`. With `express.json()` and no custom error handler, what does the client get?
choices: A 400, because the parser calls next(err) with status 400
A 500, because JSON.parse threw inside the middleware
A 200, with req.body set to undefined in the route
A 422, because the body failed schema validation
questions.why: body-parser catches the SyntaxError and forwards it with `status: 400` and `type: 'entity.parse.failed'`; Express's default handler uses that status. Your own error handler should respect `err.status` too, or every malformed body turns into a 500 and pages someone at night.
questions.asked: Shows you know that error objects carry status and your handler should not flatten everything to 500.

questions.q: In Express 5, what happens when `/report` is requested?
choices: The error handler replies handled, because Express 5 catches it
Express replies with its default 500 page and logs the stack
The request hangs, but the process stays up and keeps serving
The process crashes with an uncaught exception from the callback
questions.why: Express 5 only forwards synchronous throws and rejected promises returned by the handler. A throw inside a later callback happens on a fresh stack Express is not on, so it becomes an uncaught exception. Call `next(err)` in the callback, or use `fs/promises` and `await`.
questions.asked: Separates people who know why Express 5 catches async errors from those who think it catches everything.

questions.q: Why does this error handler check `res.headersSent`?
choices: To skip logging errors for requests that were already answered
Because a response that started streaming cannot get a new status
Because Express 5 requires it before any call to res.status()
To send the 500 only when the client has not yet disconnected
questions.why: Once headers are on the wire you cannot send a different status or body. Delegating to Express's default handler makes it destroy the socket, so the client sees an aborted response rather than a truncated one that looks complete. It is not a disconnect check and not a v5 requirement.
questions.asked: A detail from the Express docs that shows you have written an error handler for streaming responses.

questions.q: What is `res.locals` for?
choices: Values scoped to one request, shared with later middleware and views
Values shared by every request, such as config loaded at startup
Response headers that Express will send when the handler finishes
Cookies that will be set on the client once the response is sent
questions.why: `res.locals` is a fresh object per request; middleware can put the authenticated user or a request id there for later handlers and template rendering. App-wide values belong on `app.locals`, which is shared by every request and so must never hold per-user data.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know request-scoped state from app-scoped state.

questions.q: An auth middleware sets `req.user`. In a TypeScript Express app, how do you make `req.user` type-check in every handler?
choices: Cast in each handler: (req as AuthedRequest).user
Annotate the middleware as RequestHandler<User> so it flows on
Augment Express.Request with declaration merging in a .d.ts file
Add user to res.locals instead, since that is typed as any
questions.why: Declaring `interface Request { user?: User }` inside `declare global { namespace Express { ... } }` merges the property into every handler's `req` type. Casting everywhere hides mistakes, and `RequestHandler`'s first type argument is route params, not extra request properties.
questions.asked: Common in TypeScript Express codebases; shows you know declaration merging has a real use.

questions.q: A request to `/orders` never gets a response and the client eventually times out. The logs show the auth middleware ran. What is the likely bug?
choices: The auth middleware called next() twice on the same request
The auth middleware neither responded nor called next()
The route is registered with app.use instead of app.get
express.json() was registered after the auth middleware
questions.why: Express only moves on when a middleware calls `next()` or ends the response; if a branch does neither (often a missed `else` or a forgotten `next()` after an async check), the request just waits. Calling `next()` twice causes "headers already sent" errors, not a hang.
questions.asked: The first thing to suspect when requests hang; interviewers want to hear you would check every branch.

questions.q: A router is mounted with `app.use('/api', router)`. For `GET /api/orders?x=1`, what are `req.path` and `req.originalUrl` inside the router?
choices: /api/orders and /api/orders
/orders and /api/orders?x=1
/orders and /orders?x=1
/api/orders and /orders?x=1
questions.why: Mounting strips the mount path, so inside the router `req.path` and `req.url` start at `/orders`, and `req.baseUrl` is `/api`. `req.originalUrl` keeps the full URL including the query string, which is what access logs and redirects should use.
questions.asked: Relevant when logging, building links or writing auth checks inside mounted routers.

questions.q: In Express 5, `ordersRouter` is mounted at `/users/:userId/orders`. Why is `req.params.userId` undefined inside it?
choices: Routers do not inherit parent params unless created with mergeParams
Mount paths cannot contain parameters, so userId never matches
Params are only available after express.json() has run
The value is on req.query.userId once a router is mounted
questions.why: Each router has its own `req.params`, populated from its own route paths. `express.Router({ mergeParams: true })` makes it merge the parent's params in. Mount paths can contain parameters, which is why the route matched at all.
questions.asked: The standard gotcha with nested resources such as /users/:id/orders.

questions.q: What is the difference between `app.use('/admin', mw)` and `app.all('/admin', mw)`?
choices: use runs for every HTTP method; all runs for GET and POST only
use runs before routes; all runs after routes have matched
use matches /admin only; all also matches /admin/anything
use matches /admin and anything under it; all matches /admin only
questions.why: `app.use` matches the path as a prefix on segment boundaries, so `/admin/stats` runs the middleware but `/administrator` does not. `app.all` is a route for every method on the exact path. Both run for all methods; ordering depends only on registration order.
questions.asked: Checks you know why auth for a whole area goes on app.use or router.use.

questions.q: What does the client receive?
choices: Status 204 and the body {"ok":true}
Status 204 with an empty body
Status 200, because a body was sent
A 500: 204 responses cannot call json()
questions.why: 204 No Content means there is no body, so Node's HTTP layer drops whatever you write and Express strips the Content-Type. Nothing throws and the status is not upgraded to 200. If the client needs data, return 200 with the body instead.
questions.asked: Catches the "the frontend never sees my success flag" bug and checks you know what 204 means.

questions.q: After a successful HTML form POST that creates an order, which call sends the browser to the new order page as a GET?
choices: res.redirect(301, '/orders/7')
res.redirect(307, '/orders/7')
res.redirect(303, '/orders/7')
res.location('/orders/7').end()
questions.why: 303 See Other tells the client to fetch the new location with GET, which is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern that stops a refresh resubmitting the form. 307 preserves the POST method and body, 301 is permanent and cacheable, and a bare Location without a 3xx status is not a redirect.
questions.asked: Post/Redirect/Get is basic server-rendered CRUD; knowing 303 vs 307 shows HTTP fluency.

questions.q: In Express 5, what is `req.params` for `GET /files/a/b/c.txt`?
questions.code: app.get('/files/*splat', (req, res) => res.json(req.params));
choices: { splat: 'a/b/c.txt' }
{ splat: ['a', 'b', 'c.txt'] }
{ splat: 'c.txt' }
questions.why: Named wildcards in Express 5 capture one or more segments as an array of strings. Express 4 put the unnamed `*` match in `req.params[0]` as one string, which is the tempting answer. Join the segments yourself, and still guard against `..` before touching the filesystem.
questions.asked: Shows hands-on v5 experience; code that assumed a string breaks subtly on upgrade.

questions.q: A handler does `res.json({ id: 10n })` because a Postgres BIGINT came back as a BigInt. What happens?
choices: It sends {"id":10} since Express converts BigInt to Number
It sends {"id":"10"} since Express serialises BigInt as a string
It throws a TypeError, because JSON.stringify cannot serialise BigInt
It sends {"id":10n}, which the client fails to parse as JSON
questions.why: `res.json` uses `JSON.stringify`, which throws "Do not know how to serialize a BigInt". Decide on a representation (usually a string, because JS numbers lose precision past 2^53) and map it in your response DTO. Express applies no BigInt conversion of its own.
questions.asked: Real bug with BIGINT ids and ORMs; shows you think about the wire format of your DTOs.

questions.q: Which statement about Express routing with default settings is true?
choices: Paths are case-sensitive, so /Users and /users are different routes
A trailing slash is significant, so /users/ does not match /users
A GET route also answers HEAD requests, without a body
A POST to a GET-only path gets 405 Method Not Allowed
questions.why: Express answers HEAD by running the GET handler and discarding the body. Routing is case-insensitive and non-strict by default, so `/Users/` matches `/users`. A wrong method gets a 404, not 405; if you want 405 with an `Allow` header you have to add it yourself.
questions.asked: Probes whether you know Express defaults rather than assuming REST-correct behaviour.

questions.q: Express sends `ETag: W/"5-qvTG..."` on a GET. The browser repeats the request with `If-None-Match` set to that value. What does Express do by default?
choices: Sends 200 with the full body, since ETags are only used by CDNs
Runs the handler, then sends 304 with no body if the ETag matches
Skips the handler entirely and sends 304 from its response cache
Sends 412 Precondition Failed, because the ETag is only weak
questions.why: Express generates a weak ETag from the body in `res.send`, and if the request is fresh it replaces the response with a 304. The handler still runs and still queries the database; only bandwidth is saved. Express has no response cache, and 412 applies to If-Match on writes.
questions.asked: Checks you know what ETags save and what they do not, a common caching follow-up.

questions.q: Why do many teams call `app.disable('x-powered-by')`?
choices: It stops Express advertising itself in an X-Powered-By header
It disables Express's default error page in production
It turns off automatic ETag generation for every response
It stops Express trusting X-Forwarded-For from any client
questions.why: Express adds `X-Powered-By: Express` to every response. Removing it is minor hardening: it makes fingerprinting slightly harder and saves bytes. `helmet()` removes it as well. ETags, error pages and proxy trust are separate settings.
questions.asked: A small hardening detail often raised in security-flavoured Express questions.

questions.q: You want errors in RFC 9457 format. What Content-Type does this send?
choices: application/json; charset=utf-8, because json() overwrites it
text/html, because res.type expects a file extension
application/problem+json; charset=utf-8
application/problem+json, with no charset parameter
questions.why: `res.json` only sets `application/json` when no Content-Type is already present, so the earlier `res.type` survives and Express appends a charset. That makes this the idiomatic way to send Problem Details from Express. `res.type` accepts full MIME types as well as extensions.
questions.asked: Shows you can produce standard error responses rather than an ad-hoc shape.

questions.q: A Stripe webhook route must verify a signature over the exact bytes received. The app uses `app.use(express.json())` globally. What is the fix?
choices: Call JSON.stringify(req.body) and verify the signature over that
Register the webhook route with express.raw() before express.json()
Increase the express.json() limit so that the body is not truncated
Read req.rawBody, which express.json() stores alongside req.body
questions.why: Re-serialising a parsed object does not reproduce the original bytes (key order and whitespace differ), so the signature fails. Mount that route with `express.raw({ type: 'application/json' })` ahead of the global parser to get a Buffer. Express does not keep a `req.rawBody` unless you add a `verify` hook.
questions.asked: A real integration bug; knowing the fix shows you have wired payment webhooks before.

questions.q: Which event do you listen for to write an access log line with the final status code and duration?
choices: req.on('end'), which fires once the request body is fully read
res.on('close'), which fires only when the client aborts early
res.on('finish'), when the response is handed off to the OS
app.on('response'), which Express emits after every handler
questions.why: `finish` fires once the last byte of the response has been handed to the OS, so `res.statusCode` is final. `close` fires when the underlying connection closes, including after normal completion, so it is not only for aborts. Express emits no app-level 'response' event.
questions.asked: Checks you could write request-logging middleware yourself rather than only install morgan.

questions.q: With Express 5 defaults, what does `app.use(express.urlencoded())` put in `req.body` for the form body `a[b]=1&c=2`?
questions.why: Express 5 changed the `extended` default to false, so forms are parsed with `querystring`: bracket keys stay flat and every value is a string. `extended: true` uses `qs` and nests them. Neither parser turns strings into numbers; that is your validation layer's job.
questions.asked: Probes whether you know form values are strings and that v5 changed the parser default.

questions.q: In Express 5, what does `err` hold when the port is already in use?
choices: Nothing: the callback only runs on success, and the error crashes
An error with code EADDRINUSE, passed to the listen callback
Nothing: Express silently picks the next free port instead
A string message, because Express wraps errors for logging
questions.why: Express 5 forwards the server's `error` event to the `listen` callback, so a taken port arrives as an error with code `EADDRINUSE`. In Express 4 the callback was only a `listening` listener and the error was an unhandled `error` event. Neither version picks another port.
questions.asked: A small v5 change that matters for startup error handling in scripts and tests.

questions.q: A route validates the body with `z.object({ name: z.string() }).parse(req.body)`. The client sends `{ "name": "Ann", "isAdmin": true }`. What does `parse` return in Zod 4?
choices: { name: 'Ann' }, since unknown keys are stripped
{ name: 'Ann', isAdmin: true }, unchanged
Nothing: it throws because isAdmin is unknown
{ name: 'Ann', isAdmin: undefined }
questions.why: By default `z.object` strips keys it does not declare, which protects you from mass assignment when the parsed object goes straight to the database. `.strict()` (or `z.strictObject`) rejects unknown keys instead, and `.passthrough()`/`z.looseObject` keeps them.
questions.asked: Connects validation to mass assignment, which is what interviewers want you to notice.

questions.q: An endpoint accepts `?includeArchived=false` and validates it with `z.coerce.boolean()`. What value does the handler get?
choices: false, because coerce understands the string "false"
A ZodError, since "false" is not a boolean literal
undefined, because query strings cannot carry booleans
true, because Boolean("false") is true for any non-empty string
questions.why: `z.coerce.boolean()` just calls `Boolean(input)`, and every non-empty string is truthy. For query flags use `z.stringbool()` (Zod 4), which maps "true"/"false"/"1"/"0" and similar, or an explicit enum. It is a real bug: the archive filter silently inverts.
questions.asked: A sharp-edged detail that shows you have actually validated query strings, not only JSON bodies.

questions.q: What does this return for `GET /orders?page=2`?
questions.code:
const Query = z.object({ page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1) });
app.get('/orders', (req, res) => res.json(Query.parse(req.query)));
choices: {"page":"2"}, because query values are always strings
{"page":1}, because the default wins over the query value
{"page":2}, coerced from the string and checked as an integer
A 500, because z.coerce cannot run on an Express query object
questions.why: Query values arrive as strings, so `z.coerce.number()` converts "2" to 2 before `.int().min(1)` validate it; `.default(1)` only applies when the key is missing. Without coercion the schema would reject "2" as the wrong type.
questions.asked: Pagination parameters are in every CRUD API; this checks you validate and type them.

questions.q: A `GET /users/:id` handler returns `res.json(await db.user.findUnique({ where: { id } }))`. What is the main problem?
choices: It returns the whole row, including fields like passwordHash
res.json cannot serialise objects that come from an ORM
findUnique returns a promise, and res.json does not await it
Route params must be parsed by express.json() before use
questions.why: Sending the database row couples your API to your schema and leaks every column, including secrets added later. Map to a response DTO (or `select` only public fields). The await is present, ORM results are plain objects, and params never go through the body parser.
questions.asked: The standard reason for response DTOs, asked in almost every API design discussion.

questions.q: A handler does `const id = Number(req.params.id)` and passes it to the database. What happens for `GET /orders/abc` if nothing else checks it?
choices: Express rejects it with a 400, because params are typed
Number returns NaN, which reaches the query as an invalid id
Number throws a TypeError, which Express turns into a 500
Number returns 0, which fetches the first order in the table
questions.why: `Number('abc')` is `NaN`; it does not throw, and Express does no param typing. Depending on the driver you get a 500 or an odd query. Validate params with a schema (`z.coerce.number().int().positive()`) and return 400. Note `Number('')` is 0, another reason not to hand-roll it.
questions.asked: Checks you validate route params as carefully as bodies.

questions.q: With Zod, why write `type CreateOrder = z.infer<typeof CreateOrderSchema>` instead of a separate interface?
choices: z.infer makes the TypeScript type enforce the rules at runtime
Interfaces cannot describe objects that arrive over the network
The runtime schema and the static type cannot drift apart
Zod refuses to parse into a type it did not generate itself
questions.why: With one schema as the source of truth, adding a field updates both validation and the type. A hand-written interface compiles fine while the schema quietly disagrees. Types are erased at runtime, so the checks still come from `parse`, not from the inferred type.
questions.asked: Shows you understand that types stop at the boundary and how to keep them honest.

questions.q: Why should `ordersService.create` take a validated DTO rather than Express's `req` and `res`?
choices: Express objects cannot be passed across module boundaries
Services must be synchronous, and req and res are async
Passing req is slower, since Express copies it on each call
It can then be tested and reused with no HTTP involved
questions.why: A service that only sees plain inputs can be called from a test, a queue worker or a CLI, and its rules do not depend on HTTP details. Routes translate HTTP into a function call and back. The other options are not real constraints: req and res can be passed anywhere, but should not be.
questions.asked: The core of "how do you structure an Express API", asked in most backend interviews.

questions.q: Why do Express projects usually split `app.js` (builds the app) from `server.js` (calls `listen`)?
choices: Express 5 refuses to start when listen() is in the same module
Tests can import the app and drive it without opening a port
It lets app.js be ESM while server.js stays in CommonJS
Cluster mode needs listen() to live in a separate file
questions.why: Supertest can take the app function directly and runs it on an ephemeral in-memory server, so tests never fight over ports or leave a server running. `server.js` stays tiny: read config, build the app, listen, handle shutdown.
questions.asked: A concrete signal that you have written integration tests for an Express API.

questions.q: The environment has `ENABLE_CACHE=false`. What does this do?
choices: Skips the middleware, because Node parses "false" as false
Throws, because process.env values must be read with getEnv()
Skips the middleware, because unset and "false" are both falsy
Enables the cache, because the non-empty string "false" is truthy
questions.why: Every `process.env` value is a string (or undefined), and any non-empty string is truthy. Parse config once at startup, for example with a Zod schema using `z.stringbool()`, and pass typed values around instead of reading `process.env` everywhere.
questions.asked: An easy but telling config bug; the follow-up is "how would you centralise config?".

questions.q: Which versions does the range `^0.2.3` allow?
choices: Any 0.x.y at or above 0.2.3, since the major version is 0
Any version at or above 0.2.3 and below 1.0.0
Exactly 0.2.3, since caret ranges pin 0.x versions
Any 0.2.x at or above 0.2.3, but not 0.3.0
questions.why: Caret allows changes that do not modify the left-most non-zero part. For 0.x packages that part is the minor, so `^0.2.3` means `>=0.2.3 <0.3.0`. The reasoning is that semver treats 0.x minors as potentially breaking. It is not exact pinning; that needs `0.2.3` with no operator.
questions.asked: A follow-up to "what does ^ mean" that separates people who have read the semver rules.

questions.q: In CI, why run `npm ci` rather than `npm install`?
choices: It installs exactly what the lockfile says and fails if package.json disagrees
It skips devDependencies, so the build image ends up smaller and faster
It updates the lockfile to the newest versions allowed by the ranges
It installs packages globally, so each job can reuse the same cache
questions.why: `npm ci` deletes node_modules, installs the lockfile verbatim and errors if the lockfile and package.json are out of sync, giving reproducible builds. `npm install` may rewrite the lockfile. Skipping dev dependencies is `--omit=dev`, a separate flag.
questions.asked: Asked to check you know how builds stay reproducible.

questions.q: How do you install only runtime dependencies in a production Docker image?
choices: npm install --production-only
npm ci --omit=dev
npm ci --no-lockfile
npm prune --dev
questions.why: `--omit=dev` leaves devDependencies out; combined with `npm ci` it is reproducible too. `npm install` with `NODE_ENV=production` also omits them, which surprises people when a build step needs TypeScript. The other flags either do not exist or throw away the lockfile.
questions.asked: Checks you have built a lean Node image, a common deploy discussion.

questions.q: A React component library lists `react` under `peerDependencies`. Why not under `dependencies`?
choices: peerDependencies are installed faster, because npm caches them globally
The app must supply one shared React, not a second private copy
peerDependencies are only needed at build time, not when the app runs
npm refuses to publish packages that list react as a normal dependency
questions.why: A peer dependency says "I plug into the host's copy". Two React copies break hooks with "Invalid hook call", and two copies of a plugin host are similarly broken. npm 7+ installs peers automatically and reports conflicts; it does not make them build-only.
questions.asked: Shows you understand why duplicate packages cause bugs, not just where to type the name.

questions.q: A vulnerable version of `semver` is pulled in three levels deep, and the direct dependency has not released a fix. What is the npm-native way to force a patched version?
choices: Add semver to your own dependencies at the patched version
Edit node_modules/semver/package.json and commit the change
Set an overrides entry for semver in package.json
Run npm audit fix --force until the warning disappears
questions.why: `overrides` (npm 8.3+) replaces a package version anywhere in the tree, and the lockfile records it. Adding it as a direct dependency only installs a second copy beside the nested one. `audit fix --force` may jump semver-major versions of your direct dependencies and break things.
questions.asked: A practical supply-chain question; the strong answer mentions testing and removing the override later.

questions.q: What does `npm audit fix --force` risk that plain `npm audit fix` does not?
choices: It uploads your lockfile to the registry for analysis
It installs semver-major upgrades that may break your code
It removes the vulnerable packages with no replacement
It disables npm audit checks in CI from then on
questions.why: Plain `audit fix` stays within your declared ranges. `--force` will move a dependency across a major version to reach a fixed release, which can change APIs. Run the tests after any audit fix, and read the advisory: many are unreachable in your use.
questions.asked: Checks that you treat dependency updates as code changes.

questions.q: What does `npx prisma migrate dev` do if Prisma is in your devDependencies?
choices: Downloads the latest Prisma into a temporary cache and runs it
Runs the prisma binary from node_modules/.bin in your project
Installs Prisma globally, then runs the globally installed copy
Fails, because npx only runs packages that are not installed
questions.why: npx prefers the local binary in `node_modules/.bin`, so everyone runs the version pinned by the lockfile. It only downloads to a cache when the command is not installed. npm scripts get the same `.bin` folder on their PATH, which is why `"migrate": "prisma migrate dev"` works.
questions.asked: A warm-up that checks you know where CLI tools come from in a Node project.

questions.q: You run `npm run test -- --watch`. What does the `--` do?
choices: Passes --watch through to the command in the test script
Tells npm to run the test script with a watcher of its own
Runs the pretest script in watch mode before the tests start
Marks --watch as an npm flag rather than one for the script
questions.why: Everything after `--` is appended to the script's command line, so `"test": "vitest"` runs `vitest --watch`. Without the separator npm tries to interpret the flag itself. npm has no built-in watcher.
questions.asked: Everyday npm usage; interviewers use it to check hands-on experience.

questions.q: What does the `engines` field in package.json do, for example `"engines": { "node": ">=22" }`?
choices: Downloads a matching Node version before any npm script runs
Picks which Node binary npm uses for this project's scripts
Documents the supported Node versions; npm warns on a mismatch
Makes npm compile the package's code for that Node version
questions.why: npm warns when the running Node does not match, and only fails installs when `engine-strict` is set. It never downloads or switches Node; use nvm, fnm, Volta or `.nvmrc` for that. Deployment platforms often read `engines` to choose a runtime.
questions.asked: Small but practical: how do you stop a teammate running the project on an old Node.

questions.q: A package's package.json has `"exports": { ".": "./index.js" }`. What happens when you `import x from 'lib/src/internal.js'`?
choices: It works, because exports only affects require(), not import
It works, but prints a deprecation warning once per process
It works in development and fails only in a production build
Node throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED
questions.why: Once `exports` is defined it is the complete public surface: any subpath not listed is blocked, for both `import` and `require`. That is how libraries stop consumers depending on internals. Reaching in means a fork or a patch, not a workaround.
questions.asked: Checks you have hit this during an upgrade and understand package encapsulation.

questions.q: A project has `"type": "module"` in package.json. How does Node treat `server.js` and `legacy.cjs`?
choices: ES modules for each, since type applies to every file
server.js as ESM, legacy.cjs as CommonJS
CommonJS for each, until you pass --experimental-modules
server.js as CommonJS, legacy.cjs as ESM
questions.why: `"type": "module"` makes `.js` files ES modules; `.cjs` is always CommonJS and `.mjs` is always ESM, whatever the type field says. Without the field `.js` defaults to CommonJS. No flag has been needed since Node 12.
questions.asked: The basic rule behind most "Cannot use import statement outside a module" errors.

questions.q: In a Node 24 ES module, what happens here?
questions.code: const uploads = path.join(__dirname, 'uploads');
choices: It works, because Node defines __dirname in every module
It gives the working directory, not the file's directory
ReferenceError: __dirname is not defined in ES module scope
It works, but only if the file has a .mjs extension
questions.why: `__dirname`, `__filename` and `require` are CommonJS wrapper variables and do not exist in ESM. Use `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` (Node 20.11+), or `fileURLToPath(new URL('.', import.meta.url))` on older versions. `process.cwd()` is the working directory, which is a different thing.
questions.asked: The first error most people hit when moving an Express app to ESM.

questions.q: In a Node 24 ES module, `db.js` exists next to this file. What happens?
questions.code: import { pool } from './db';
choices: It works: Node tries .js, .mjs and .cjs in turn
ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND: relative ESM imports need the extension
It works only if db.js has a default export as well
It loads ./db/index.js, and fails when that is missing
questions.why: Node's ESM resolver is URL-based and does no extension guessing or directory index lookup, so you must write `./db.js`. Bundlers and TypeScript's old `node` resolution guessed extensions, which is why code that worked in a bundle fails in plain Node.
questions.asked: Common when converting a project to ESM; checks you know Node is stricter than bundlers.

questions.q: How do you load `config.json` in a Node 24 ES module?
choices: import config from './config.json';
const config = require('./config.json');
import config from './config.json' with { type: 'json' };
import * as config from './config.json?json';
questions.why: JSON modules need an import attribute; without it Node throws ERR_IMPORT_ATTRIBUTE_MISSING. `require` is not defined in ESM unless you create one with `createRequire`. The attribute exists so a server cannot swap a JSON URL for executable JavaScript.
questions.asked: Checks you know current ESM syntax rather than bundler-only conveniences.

questions.q: Why is `export const pool = new Pool(...)` in `db.js` effectively a singleton?
choices: pg detects a second Pool for the same database and reuses the first
Node evaluates a module once and caches it, so every import shares it
const exports are frozen, so no other file can create a second pool
ES modules run in their own worker thread with one shared instance
questions.why: Both module systems cache a module after its first evaluation, so every importer gets the same `pool` object. That is why a module-level pool or Prisma client is the normal pattern. `const` only stops reassignment of the binding; it does not prevent another `new Pool` elsewhere.
questions.asked: Links module caching to connection pooling, which comes up in every Node data-access question.

questions.q: What does `--env-file=.env` do in Node 24 when a variable is already set in the real environment?
questions.code:
# .env contains PORT=4000
PORT=5000 node --env-file=.env server.js
choices: process.env.PORT is 4000, since the file overrides the environment
Node refuses to start, because PORT is defined in two places
process.env.PORT is "4000,5000", as both values are merged
process.env.PORT is 5000, because the real environment wins
questions.why: Node's built-in env-file loader does not overwrite variables that are already set, matching dotenv's default. That lets a platform's real environment override a committed development file. Node has loaded .env files natively since 20.6, so dotenv is optional.
questions.asked: Checks you know the precedence rule, which decides whether prod secrets or a stale file win.

questions.q: Why validate all configuration with a schema when the process starts, rather than reading `process.env` where it is needed?
choices: process.env becomes read-only after the first request is handled
A missing or malformed value crashes at boot, not hours later
Reading process.env inside handlers leaks secrets into logs
Schema validation encrypts secrets while they sit in memory
questions.why: Failing fast turns a typo in `DATABASE_URL` into a deploy that never becomes healthy, rather than a 500 on the first request that touches the database. Parsing once also gives typed values (numbers, booleans, URLs) instead of strings scattered through the code.
questions.asked: A standard design question; the strong answer mentions readiness checks and rollbacks.

questions.q: In Node, what type does `process.env.PORT` have after `process.env.PORT = 8080`?
choices: number
string
bigint
undefined
questions.why: `process.env` coerces every assigned value to a string, so it reads back as "8080". That is why `port + 1` gives "80801". Convert once at startup (`Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000)` or a schema) and pass numbers around.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know environment variables are always strings.

questions.q: With pino, what does this line write?
questions.code: logger.error('payment failed', err);
choices: The message plus err serialised under an err key with its stack
The message only; err is treated as a format argument and dropped
Two separate log lines, one for the message and one for the error
A TypeError, because pino requires an object as its first argument
questions.why: Pino's signature is `(mergingObject?, message?, ...interpolationValues)`. A string first means extra arguments only fill `%s`-style placeholders, so the error vanishes. Write `logger.error({ err }, 'payment failed')` and pino's err serialiser records type, message and stack.
questions.asked: A real bug that silently removes stack traces from production logs.

questions.q: A pino logger is created with `level: 'info'`. What happens to `logger.debug({ order }, 'priced')`?
choices: It is written, tagged debug, for the log system to filter later
It is buffered in memory and flushed if an error is logged next
It throws, because debug is not enabled on this logger
It is discarded before the object is serialised, so it is cheap
questions.why: Below-threshold methods are no-ops, so the call costs little more than a function call. Buffer-until-error is a pattern some loggers offer but not pino's default. Change the level at runtime (for example via an env var) when you need debug output.
questions.asked: Checks you know levels are a cost control as well as a filter.

questions.q: In a pino-based Express app, what does `req.log.child({ orderId })` give you?
choices: A second log file that only contains this order's lines
A logger that adds orderId to every line it writes
A logger with a lower level, just for this request
A copy of the request object with orderId attached
questions.why: A child logger inherits the parent's bindings (such as the request id from pino-http) and adds its own, so every line carries both without repeating them at each call. It writes to the same destination and keeps the parent's level unless you set one.
questions.asked: Shows you know how to make logs searchable per request or per entity.

questions.q: Which pino option stops `Authorization` headers and passwords appearing in logs?
choices: redact: ['req.headers.authorization', '*.password']
serializers: { req: false, password: false }
level: 'secure', with secrets masked by level
transport: { target: 'pino-mask', options: {} }
questions.why: `redact` takes paths (wildcards allowed) and replaces those values with "[Redacted]" before the line is written. Serialisers customise how an object is logged but do not accept `false` to hide a key, and there is no secure level. Redaction is a safety net; avoid logging whole request bodies in the first place.
questions.asked: Leaking tokens into logs is a common incident; interviewers like a concrete prevention.

questions.q: Why is `pino-pretty` usually used only in development?
choices: It is not thread-safe, so it corrupts output under load
It requires a TTY and crashes inside Docker containers
Production log systems want the raw one-line JSON
It strips the error stack traces from logged errors
questions.why: Log collectors parse JSON lines into searchable fields; coloured, multi-line text defeats that and costs CPU. Keep the service writing JSON to stdout and pipe it through pino-pretty on your machine. It works without a TTY and keeps stacks, so those are not the reasons.
questions.asked: Checks you know logs are data for machines first.

questions.q: What does this test need to run?
choices: A server started on port 3000 before the test file runs
Nothing extra: supertest binds the app to an ephemeral port
A mock of the http module so that no socket is opened
NODE_ENV=test, because supertest refuses to run otherwise
questions.why: Given an app (a request handler function), supertest starts it on a random free port for the request and closes it afterwards. That is why exporting a `buildApp()` without calling `listen` matters. It opens real sockets on localhost; nothing is mocked.
questions.asked: The baseline API-testing question in Node interviews.

questions.q: Why can you pass an Express `app` straight to `http.createServer(app)`?
choices: Express subclasses http.Server, so app is already a server
createServer checks for Express and wraps it in an adapter
app is a function with the (req, res) request-listener shape
app exports a toServer() method that createServer calls
questions.why: An Express app is itself a function `(req, res, next)`, so it fits Node's request-listener signature. `app.listen` is literally `http.createServer(this).listen(...)`. That is also how you attach a WebSocket server to the same HTTP server.
questions.asked: Shows you understand what Express is underneath, useful for WebSocket and HTTPS setups.

questions.q: Why is `express.static('public')` registered before the auth middleware in many apps?
choices: Static files cannot be served after any middleware has run
Public assets are then served without running the auth check
Auth middleware corrupts binary file responses such as images
Express only compresses files that are served before auth runs
questions.why: Order decides who sees what: middleware registered before auth is public, after auth is protected. CSS, images and the login page must load for logged-out users, and skipping auth for them saves work. Put files that need protection behind the auth middleware or serve them through a route.
questions.asked: Another angle on "order is behaviour" that also tests basic access control.

questions.q: What does `requireRole('admin')` need to return for this to work?
questions.code: router.delete('/users/:id', requireRole('admin'), deleteUser);
choices: A boolean, which Express uses to decide whether to continue
A promise that resolves once the user's role has been checked
A middleware function (req, res, next) that closes over the role
A router, so Express can mount it in front of this route
questions.why: It is a middleware factory: calling it with the role returns a closure that checks `req.user.role` and either calls `next()` or sends 403. Express ignores return values from middleware, so a boolean does nothing, and an async function returning a promise still has to call next or respond.
questions.asked: Checks you can write parameterised middleware, a very common take-home pattern.

questions.q: What does a final `app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: 'not found' }))` do?
choices: It runs before every route and blocks paths that are unknown
It handles only thrown NotFoundError instances from routes
It sends 404 for any request that no earlier route handled
It overrides Express's 404 only when NODE_ENV=production
questions.why: A two-argument middleware at the end is only reached when nothing earlier ended the response, which is the definition of an unmatched route. It must sit after all routes and before the four-argument error handler. Thrown errors skip it and go to the error handler.
questions.asked: Checks you know how to give an API a consistent JSON 404 instead of Express's HTML one.

questions.q: Services throw `new NotFoundError('order')`. What is the usual way to turn that into a 404 in Express 5?
choices: Catch it in every route and call res.status(404) by hand
Give the error a status and map it in the central error handler
Throw it with next(404) so that Express picks the status itself
Return it from the handler; Express reads the status field
questions.why: A typed error with a `status` (or a mapping in the handler) keeps services HTTP-agnostic while one place decides the response shape. Express 5 forwards the throw from an async handler. Try/catch in every route duplicates that logic, and `next(404)` passes a number, not an error.
questions.asked: The mid-level answer to "what is your error-handling strategy in an API?"

questions.q: What changes in an Express app when `NODE_ENV=production`?
choices: Express enables gzip compression and clustering automatically
The default error handler hides stacks and views get cached
Body size limits are raised, because traffic is assumed to be real
Nothing: Express ignores NODE_ENV and only libraries read it
questions.why: Express reads NODE_ENV into `app.get('env')`: in production the default error handler returns only the status message, and view templates are cached. It does not compress, cluster or change limits. Many libraries and `npm install` also behave differently, so set it everywhere you deploy.
questions.asked: Checks you know NODE_ENV has real effects, and that forgetting it leaks stack traces.

questions.q: Where should gzip or Brotli compression of API responses usually happen?
choices: In the handler, by calling zlib.gzipSync on every response body
Only on the client, since browsers decompress for free anyway
In the database driver, which compresses rows before sending
At the reverse proxy or CDN, or with compression middleware
questions.why: Compression is CPU work; a proxy or CDN does it outside your event loop and can cache the result. The `compression` middleware is a reasonable fallback. `gzipSync` in a handler blocks the event loop for every request, and the client cannot decompress what was never compressed.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about where work runs, not just whether it happens.

questions.q: An upload route uses multer with `memoryStorage()` and no limits. What is the risk?
choices: Uploaded files are written to disk with world-readable permissions
The first upload blocks all later requests until it finishes
A few huge uploads hold whole files in RAM and can exhaust memory
Multer strips the Content-Type, so every file is saved as text
questions.why: Memory storage buffers each file completely in the process's heap. Without `limits: { fileSize, files }`, a handful of large uploads can crash the service. Set limits, and for big files stream to disk or directly to object storage. Uploads are streamed asynchronously, so they do not block other requests.
questions.asked: File uploads are a standard CRUD feature and a standard denial-of-service vector.

questions.q: How do you run a different stricter rate limit on `POST /login` than on the rest of the API with express-rate-limit?
choices: Call app.use(limiter) twice; Express keeps the stricter of the two
Set the rate limit in express.json() options for the login route
Put the login route in its own process with its own global limit
Pass a dedicated limiter as middleware on that route only
questions.why: Limiters are ordinary middleware, so `app.post('/login', loginLimiter, login)` applies a tighter window just there while a looser global limiter covers everything else. Two global `app.use` calls both run; nothing picks the stricter one, and body-parser has no rate options.
questions.asked: Brute-force protection on login is expected knowledge for anyone building auth.

questions.q: Which statement about cookies in Express 5 is correct?
choices: res.cookie() is built in; reading req.cookies needs cookie-parser
res.cookie() and req.cookies each need the cookie-parser package
req.cookies is built in; setting cookies needs express-session
Express 5 removed cookies in favour of the Set-Cookie header
questions.why: `res.cookie(name, value, options)` ships with Express and writes the Set-Cookie header. Parsing the incoming Cookie header into `req.cookies` (and verifying signed cookies) is done by the `cookie-parser` middleware. express-session manages its own cookie separately.
questions.asked: Checks hands-on familiarity with the Express request and response APIs.

questions.q: What does a signed cookie from `cookie-parser` protect against?
choices: The client reading the value, because it is encrypted
The client changing the value without detection
Scripts in the page reading the cookie via document.cookie
The cookie being sent over plain HTTP connections
questions.why: A signed cookie carries an HMAC of the value using your secret; a tampered value fails verification and shows up as false in `req.signedCookies`. The value itself is still readable, so do not put secrets in it. Script access and transport are controlled by `httpOnly` and `secure`.
questions.asked: Signing versus encryption is a frequent security clarification.

questions.q: Which Express typing lets TypeScript check `req.params.id` and `req.body.qty` in a route handler?
choices: Request<{ id: string }, unknown, { qty: number }>
Request<{ qty: number }, { id: string }>
Request & { params: { id: number } }
RequestHandler<{ id: number; qty: number }>
questions.why: Express's `Request` generics are, in order: route params, response body, request body, query. Params are always strings in the types because they are strings at runtime. The annotation is still a claim, not a check, so the body must be validated before you trust `qty`.
questions.asked: Common in TypeScript backends; the strong answer adds that the generic is not validation.

questions.q: You use `app.route('/orders').get(list).post(create)`. What does `app.route` give you?
choices: A separate router with its own middleware stack and error handler
One path declared once, with method handlers chained on it
Automatic 405 responses for methods that you have not declared
A route that is registered lazily, on the first matching request
questions.why: `app.route(path)` returns a single Route so you can chain `.get`, `.post` and so on without repeating the path string, which avoids typos. It is not a separate router and does not add 405 handling; unmatched methods still fall through to 404.
questions.asked: A small API-surface question that tells the interviewer you have read Express code.

questions.q: What does `node --watch server.js` do in Node 24?
choices: Restarts the process when an imported file changes
Hot-swaps changed functions without restarting the process
Runs server.js under nodemon, if nodemon is installed
Watches the event loop and logs any blocking operations
questions.why: Watch mode (stable since Node 22) restarts the process when the entry file or anything it imports changes, which replaces nodemon for most projects. It is a restart, not hot module replacement, so in-memory state is lost each time.
questions.asked: Checks your tooling knowledge is current with built-in Node features.

questions.q: In Node 24, you run `node server.ts` directly. Which of these makes it fail?
choices: An interface declaration used as a type annotation
A generic function such as function first<T>(xs: T[])
An enum declaration, such as enum Status { Open }
A type-only import written as import type { User }
questions.why: Node runs TypeScript by stripping erasable syntax, replacing types with whitespace. Enums, namespaces and parameter properties generate runtime code, so Node throws ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX. Use a const object plus a union type, or enable `erasableSyntaxOnly` in tsconfig to catch it at compile time.
questions.asked: Checks you know what native TypeScript in Node does and does not do.

questions.q: In Node 24 with native type stripping, why does this crash with "does not provide an export named 'User'"?
choices: Node needs the .js extension on TypeScript imports, even for .ts files
Interfaces are erased, so the runtime import asks for a missing export
Stripping only works in CommonJS files, not in ES modules
Exported interfaces must be declared with export type instead
questions.why: Type stripping does not know that `User` is only a type, so the import stays and the ES module linker finds no such export. Write `import type { User }` (and turn on `verbatimModuleSyntax` so tsc enforces it). Node resolves `.ts` extensions as written, so the path is fine.
questions.asked: A current gotcha that shows you have actually run TypeScript on Node without a build step.

questions.q: What does `GET /download` return in Express 5?
questions.code: app.get('/download', (req, res) => res.sendFile('reports/latest.pdf'));
