choices: The file, resolved against the current working directory
The file, resolved against the directory of the calling module
An error: the path must be absolute or you must pass a root option
A 404, because sendFile only serves files from express.static roots
questions.why: `res.sendFile` refuses relative paths, which avoids resolving against whatever the working directory happens to be. Pass `{ root: import.meta.dirname }` or an absolute path. With `root`, Express also rejects `..` segments, which helps against path traversal.
questions.asked: Common first-use error, and a chance to mention path traversal safety.

questions.q: A client sends `Accept: image/png` to this route. What happens?
choices: Express sends the JSON, since it is the first entry listed
Express sends the HTML, since browsers always accept it
The request hangs, since neither callback is ever called
Express passes a 406 Not Acceptable error to next()
questions.why: `res.format` negotiates against the Accept header; when nothing matches and there is no `default` callback it forwards a 406 error. Add a `default` entry if you would rather fall back to JSON. Without an Accept header at all, the first entry wins.
questions.asked: Content negotiation comes up when one route serves both a browser and an API client.

questions.q: In an integration test, why use `request.agent(app)` instead of `request(app)` for a login-then-fetch flow?
choices: The agent reuses a single TCP port, so the tests run faster
The agent keeps cookies between requests, like a browser
The agent follows redirects, which plain request() never does
The agent starts the app once and keeps it listening afterwards
questions.why: A supertest agent stores Set-Cookie responses and sends them on later requests, so a session cookie from `POST /login` authenticates `GET /me`. Separate `request(app)` calls share nothing. Redirect following is opt-in with `.redirects(n)` on either.
questions.asked: Checks you can test authenticated routes realistically rather than bypassing auth.

questions.q: A body fails validation on two fields. What does `schema.safeParse(body)` return in Zod 4?
choices: { success: false, error } with an issue for each failing field
{ success: false, error } with only the first failing field
It throws a ZodError that lists both of the failing fields
null, with the individual issues logged to the console
questions.why: Zod collects every issue in one pass, so the client can fix all fields at once; `safeParse` returns a result object instead of throwing. `z.flattenError(error)` or `z.treeifyError(error)` reshape the issues into a per-field form for a 400 response.
questions.asked: Checks you know how to return all field errors, which frontends need for forms.

questions.q: You write a `validate(schema)` middleware. What should it do when parsing succeeds?
choices: Call next() and leave req.body untouched, so handlers can re-parse it
Send 200 at once, since the request body is now known to be valid
Store the parsed result (req.body or res.locals) and call next()
Throw a sentinel error that the router treats as a success signal
questions.why: The parsed output is the valuable part: unknown keys stripped, strings coerced, defaults applied. Replace `req.body` (writable) or put the result on `res.locals`; `req.query` is a getter in Express 5, so it cannot be reassigned. Leaving the raw body means handlers work with unvalidated data.
questions.asked: Writing this middleware is a common take-home task; the detail is keeping the parsed output.

questions.q: What does `app.param('id', loadOrder)` do?
choices: Declares that :id must be numeric in every route of the app
Runs loadOrder whenever a route with an :id parameter matches
Renames the :id route parameter to loadOrder in req.params
Adds id to req.query when a route does not define it
questions.why: `app.param` registers a callback `(req, res, next, value)` that runs once per request before the handlers of any route containing that parameter, often used to load the entity or 404. It does no type validation on its own; you still check the value inside the callback.
questions.asked: A less common Express feature; knowing it shows depth, and the trade-off is hidden control flow.

questions.q: What does the client receive from `res.json(undefined)` in Express 5?
choices: A 500, because undefined cannot be serialised
The string "undefined" with a text/plain type
A 204 No Content with no Content-Type header
A 200 with an empty body and a JSON Content-Type
questions.why: `JSON.stringify(undefined)` returns undefined, so Express sends an empty body while still labelling it JSON, and `response.json()` in the client throws on it. It usually means a missing `return` or `await`. Return `null`, a 404 or a 204 deliberately instead.
questions.asked: Shows you can diagnose the "Unexpected end of JSON input" error from the server side.

questions.q: In CommonJS, why does `exports = { createOrder }` export nothing?
choices: It rebinds the local exports variable, not module.exports
exports is read-only, so the assignment throws silently
Object literals must be exported with export default
The export only takes effect after the first require()
questions.why: `exports` starts as a reference to `module.exports`; reassigning it points the local variable elsewhere and `require` still returns the original empty object. Write `module.exports = { ... }` or add properties with `exports.createOrder = ...`.
questions.asked: A classic CommonJS question that still shows up in codebases being migrated.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: undefined
A TypeError
questions.why: ES module imports are live bindings to the exporter's variable, so the importer sees the updated value 2. CommonJS `const { n } = require(...)` copies the value at require time and would log 1. The importer still cannot assign to `n` itself.
questions.asked: Probes whether you understand ESM beyond syntax, relevant when migrating CommonJS code.

questions.q: When is a dynamic `await import('./reports/pdf.js')` a good choice in a Node service?
choices: Always, because dynamic imports are cached while static imports are not
When the module is heavy and only some requests or commands need it
When the module is CommonJS, which static import cannot load in Node
When you need the import to run synchronously before the app starts
questions.why: Dynamic import defers loading until the code path runs, which trims startup time and memory for rarely used, heavy dependencies. Both forms are cached. Static `import` can load CommonJS, and dynamic import is asynchronous, not synchronous.
questions.asked: Checks you know import() is a tool for lazy loading, not a module-system workaround.

questions.q: What does an npm workspace setup (`"workspaces": ["packages/*"]`) give a monorepo?
choices: Each package gets its own lockfile and separate node_modules
Packages are published together as one tarball to the registry
One install links local packages to each other, with one lockfile
Local packages are copied into each other's dist folder on build
questions.why: Workspaces install everything from the root with one lockfile and symlink local packages into node_modules, so `api` can depend on `shared` without publishing it. Run scripts per package with `npm run build -w shared`. Nothing is copied or bundled together.
questions.asked: Monorepos with a shared types package are common in fullstack TypeScript shops.

questions.q: You get a merge conflict in package-lock.json. What is the usual fix?
choices: Delete the lockfile and commit the result of a fresh npm install
Resolve package.json, then run npm install to regenerate the lock
Keep whichever side has more lines, then run npm ci to confirm
Add package-lock.json to .gitignore so the conflict cannot recur
questions.why: npm can resolve lockfile conflict markers itself: fix package.json first, then `npm install` rewrites a consistent lockfile. Deleting the lockfile re-resolves every transitive dependency, pulling in untested versions, and ignoring it loses reproducible installs.
questions.asked: An everyday team-work question; the wrong answer (delete it) is a real red flag.

questions.q: You publish a library that has a committed package-lock.json. What do consumers get?
choices: Your exact dependency versions, since the lock is published with it
Whatever their resolver picks within your package.json ranges
An install error if their lockfile disagrees with yours
Your locked versions in development and theirs in production
questions.why: package-lock.json is not honoured for dependencies: the consumer's own lockfile governs the whole tree, resolved from your declared ranges. That is why libraries must test against their range, not just their lock. `npm-shrinkwrap.json` is the rarely appropriate exception.
questions.asked: Separates application and library thinking about dependency locking.

questions.q: What does `npm outdated` show?
choices: Packages with known vulnerabilities, grouped by severity
Installed versions next to the wanted and latest versions
Packages that no longer receive updates from their authors
Dependencies listed in package.json that are never imported
questions.why: `npm outdated` lists current, wanted (highest version within your range) and latest for each dependency. Vulnerabilities come from `npm audit`, and unused dependencies need a tool such as knip or depcheck. It is the starting point for a routine upgrade.
questions.asked: A practical warm-up about keeping dependencies healthy.

questions.q: How should a service tell production from staging for its own feature switches?
choices: Read NODE_ENV, setting it to staging on the staging servers
Detect the hostname at startup and compare it to a known list
Keep separate git branches with hard-coded values per stage
Use explicit settings such as APP_ENV or per-feature variables
questions.why: NODE_ENV is a build/runtime mode that libraries read ("production" enables optimisations); staging should run with NODE_ENV=production so it behaves like prod. Deployment identity and feature switches belong in their own variables. Hostname checks and per-branch code are brittle.
questions.asked: A common confusion; the strong answer is "staging should be production-like".

questions.q: Where should a Node service in Kubernetes or a PaaS get its database password?
choices: From a .env file committed next to the Dockerfile
From a secret store, injected as an env var or file
Hard-coded in config.ts, since the image is private
From a query-string parameter on the health check
questions.why: Secrets live in a managed store (Kubernetes Secrets, a cloud secret manager, Vault) and reach the process at runtime as environment variables or mounted files. Anything baked into the image or the repo is visible to everyone with read access and lasts forever in history.
questions.asked: Basic secret hygiene is checked in almost every backend interview.

questions.q: What does `pino-http` add to an Express app?
choices: A request logger that attaches req.log and logs each response
A transport that ships logs to a hosted service over HTTP
Middleware that hides HTTP headers from all log output
An HTTP endpoint for changing the log level at runtime
questions.why: pino-http creates a child logger per request (with a request id) at `req.log`, and writes one line per completed response with method, url, status and response time. Shipping logs is the platform's job, and redaction is configured, not automatic.
questions.asked: Shows you know the standard Node logging stack, not just console.log.

questions.q: A request arrives with `x-request-id: abc123` from the gateway. Why should your logger use that id rather than generate a new one?
choices: Generated ids would collide once several instances are running
Express rejects requests that carry an id you did not generate
So one search finds the request in every service's logs
Pino can only index ids that come from request headers
questions.why: Propagating the incoming id (and forwarding it on outgoing calls) correlates one user action across the gateway, your API and downstream services. Generate one only when the header is missing, and trust it only from your own infrastructure. UUIDs do not collide in practice.
questions.asked: Correlation ids are the core of debugging distributed requests.

questions.q: Which of these is fine to log at info level for a login request?
choices: The request body, so failed logins can be replayed for debugging
The user id and outcome, with the password and token left out
The Authorization header, trimmed to its first 20 characters
The password hash, since hashes cannot be reversed
questions.why: Log who, what and the result; never credentials, tokens or hashes. Request bodies contain passwords, a partial bearer token can still be enough to use, and leaked hashes can be cracked offline. Logs are copied to many systems with weaker access controls than your database.
questions.asked: Tests basic judgement about sensitive data, which interviewers weigh heavily.

questions.q: In Node 24's built-in test runner, what does this do?
choices: Replaces every send() call in the process with the fake
Creates a spy function and checks it was called once
Stubs the network so that notifyUser makes no requests
Fails, because mock.fn needs a --experimental flag
questions.why: `mock.fn` returns a tracked function you pass in as a dependency; `mock.calls` and `callCount()` record how it was used. It affects only code that receives it, which is why injecting dependencies makes Node code easy to test. The mocking API is stable and needs no flag.
questions.asked: Checks you can test Node code without installing Jest or Vitest.

questions.q: An API test suite shares one database. Tests pass alone but fail when run together. What is the usual cause?
choices: Supertest opens too many sockets once there are many tests
Node caches HTTP responses between separate test files
Express keeps route state between separate buildApp() calls
Tests leave or depend on rows that other tests also touch
questions.why: Shared data couples tests: one inserts a user with the same email another expects to create, or counts rows another test added. Reset or truncate between tests, wrap each in a rolled-back transaction, or give each test unique data. Node and supertest do not cache responses.
questions.asked: Test isolation is one of the most common reasons API suites become flaky.

questions.q: Why pass dependencies into `buildApp({ ordersRepo, mailer })` rather than importing them at the top of each route file?
choices: Express only accepts services that are passed into buildApp()
Tests can pass fakes without module-mocking tricks
Imports are slower than function arguments at runtime
It lets each route choose its own database connection
questions.why: Manual dependency injection keeps the wiring in one place: production passes real implementations, tests pass in-memory fakes or a test database. Hard imports force module mocking, which is fragile with ESM. Performance is not the reason.
questions.asked: The Node answer to "how do you do dependency injection without a framework?"

questions.q: Which folder layout scales best as an Express API grows past a dozen resources?
choices: By feature: orders/ holds its routes, schema, service and repository
By type: routes/, services/ and repositories/ at the top level
One file per HTTP method: get.js, post.js, put.js and delete.js
Everything in app.js, split only when a file reaches 5,000 lines
questions.why: Feature folders keep everything a change touches together, so adding a field to orders edits one folder, and a feature can be moved or deleted as a unit. Layer-first folders work for small apps but spread each change across the tree. Either is defensible; the reasoning is what interviewers want.
questions.asked: Opinion-with-reasons question; interviewers want trade-offs, not a single right answer.

questions.q: Why map a database row to a response object with a function like `toOrderDto(row)` before sending it?
choices: Express refuses to send objects with prototype methods attached
The API contract stops changing whenever the schema changes
It is required before res.json() can apply compression
Database rows are immutable, so they must be copied first
questions.why: A mapping layer decides exactly which fields leave the server and in what shape, so a column rename or a new secret column does not silently change or leak through the API. It is also where you format dates, BigInts and money consistently.
questions.asked: The "why DTOs" question that appears in both Node and .NET interviews.

questions.q: Why validate `limit` with something like `z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100)` on a list endpoint?
choices: So one request cannot ask for millions of rows at once
Because Postgres rejects LIMIT values above 100 by default
Because Express caps query numbers at 100 unless configured
So the response can be cached by the CDN under a fixed key
questions.why: Without a cap, `?limit=1000000` makes the database, the server and the network do enormous work for one request, which is an easy denial-of-service. Postgres and Express impose no such limits. Pick a sensible default and a maximum.
questions.asked: Pagination input is a standard place to check defensive thinking.

questions.q: With `express-session`, what does `saveUninitialized: false` do?
choices: It refuses to create sessions for users who are not logged in
It avoids storing a session or setting a cookie until one is modified
It keeps sessions in memory only, so they never reach the store
It stops the session cookie being sent over plain HTTP connections
questions.why: With `saveUninitialized: false`, anonymous visitors who never touch `req.session` get no row in the store and no cookie, which saves storage and helps with cookie-consent rules. It does not enforce login, pick the store, or set `secure`; those are separate options.
questions.asked: Checks you have configured sessions rather than copy-pasting options.

questions.q: Behind a TLS-terminating load balancer, session cookies with `cookie: { secure: true }` are never set. Why?
choices: Secure cookies need a signed certificate on the Node process itself
Load balancers strip every Set-Cookie header by default
Express sees plain HTTP from the balancer unless trust proxy is set
Secure cookies only work when sameSite is also set to none
questions.why: express-session only sets a secure cookie when `req.secure` is true. Behind a proxy, the connection to Node is HTTP; `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` makes Express honour `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`. Load balancers pass Set-Cookie through, and sameSite is unrelated.
questions.asked: A real deploy-day bug; knowing it shows you have run Express behind a proxy.

questions.q: With the `cors` package, which option lets the browser send cookies to your API from `https://app.example.com`?
choices: cors({ origin: '*', credentials: true })
cors({ origin: 'https://app.example.com', credentials: true })
cors({ origin: true, allowCookies: 'always', maxAge: 600 })
cors({ credentials: 'include', origin: 'same-site' })
questions.why: Credentialed requests require `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and a specific origin; browsers reject a wildcard origin with credentials. The client also needs `credentials: 'include'` on fetch. `origin: true` reflects any origin, which with credentials lets every site make logged-in requests.
questions.asked: CORS with cookies is a frequent integration headache for fullstack developers.

questions.q: You add `express-rate-limit` with its default memory store to an API that runs as four replicas. What is the effective limit per client?
choices: Exactly the configured limit, since replicas share the store
Zero, since replicas reject requests from unknown instances
The configured limit, but only counted on the first replica
Up to four times the limit, since each replica counts alone
questions.why: The memory store lives in each process, so a client spread across replicas by the load balancer gets a fresh allowance on each one. Use a shared store (Redis, for example via `rate-limit-redis`) for a real global limit, or enforce limits at the gateway.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about horizontal scaling when adding in-process state.

questions.q: Why does `helmet()` break an app that loads a chart library from a CDN with a `<script>` tag?
choices: Helmet blocks outbound requests from Node to CDN hosts
Its default Content-Security-Policy only allows same-origin scripts
Helmet strips script tags from HTML responses rendered by Express
The Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header blocks incoming scripts
questions.why: Helmet's default CSP includes `script-src 'self'`, so the browser refuses scripts from other origins. Add the CDN to `script-src` (ideally with Subresource Integrity) or self-host the file. CORP controls who may embed your resources, not which scripts your page loads.
questions.asked: A common first-deploy issue with helmet; the fix shows you understand CSP.

questions.q: In an Express 5 handler, how do you stop an expensive database query when the client disconnects?
choices: Nothing is needed: Express cancels pending awaits on disconnect
Listen for req 'close', abort a controller, pass its signal on
Call res.end() in a finally block to release the query early
Set server.requestTimeout to 0 so cancelled requests stop
questions.why: Node emits `close` when the connection goes away; aborting an `AbortController` there lets `fetch`, many drivers and your own loops stop work early. Express does not cancel promises, and `res.end()` only ends the response. Check `res.writableFinished` so a normal close does not abort completed work.
questions.asked: Shows awareness that abandoned requests still cost server resources.

questions.q: What does `res.end()` do differently from `res.send('')`?
choices: res.end() finishes with no Express processing such as ETag or Content-Type
res.end() keeps the connection open, while res.send() closes the socket
res.end() sets the status to 204, while res.send('') always sends 200
res.end() is asynchronous, while res.send() writes the whole body at once
questions.why: `res.end` is Node's raw ServerResponse method: it just finishes the response. `res.send` is Express sugar that sets Content-Type, Content-Length and an ETag before calling `end`. Neither changes the status on its own, and keep-alive is decided by the connection, not by which you call.
questions.asked: Checks you know where Express ends and Node's http module begins.

questions.q: A route runs `const sorted = bigArray.sort(...)` over 2 million items on every request. What does this do to other requests?
choices: Nothing: Express runs each request handler in its own thread
They slow down only if they also call sort() at the same time
They wait: the sort blocks the event loop until it finishes
Node pauses the sort to serve them, then resumes it afterwards
questions.why: Handlers run on one JavaScript thread; synchronous CPU work runs to completion and every other request, timer and health check waits. Move the work to the database, cache the result, paginate, or offload to a worker thread. Node does not pre-empt running JavaScript.
questions.asked: The practical form of "what blocks the event loop", asked in nearly every Node interview.

questions.q: Why is `app.use(express.json({ limit: '10mb' }))` a poor fix when one upload route needs large bodies?
choices: express.json ignores limits larger than 1mb
The limit then applies to every JSON route
The limit must be a number of bytes, not a string
Large limits disable the parser's JSON validation
questions.why: A global 10 MB limit lets any endpoint be fed 10 MB bodies to parse on the event loop. Keep a small global default and mount a larger parser only on the route that needs it, or stream uploads to storage. String sizes such as '10mb' are accepted.
questions.asked: Checks you scope risky settings to where they are needed.

questions.q: Where does `app.set('json spaces', 2)` belong?
choices: In production, so logs from res.json are easier to read
Nowhere: Express 5 removed the setting in favour of res.pretty()
In development only, since it pretty-prints res.json output
In tests, because supertest cannot parse compact JSON
questions.why: The setting indents every `res.json` body, which is handy when reading responses by hand but adds bytes to every response in production. Supertest and every client parse compact JSON fine. Express 5 still supports it.
questions.asked: A small check on Express settings and on thinking about payload size.

questions.q: Where should the DTO schema for `POST /orders` live in a feature-folder Express project?
choices: In the database migration that creates the orders table
In a global schemas.js shared by every feature in the app
Inside the route handler, defined again on every request
In orders/, next to the routes and service that use it
questions.why: Keeping `orders.schema.ts` beside the routes and service means one folder owns the contract, and the schema is created once at module load. Defining it inside the handler rebuilds it per request. Migrations describe storage, not the API contract, and the two should be allowed to differ.
questions.asked: Checks you keep request contracts separate from database schema.
